## Introduction

Crépon, Devoto, Duflo, and Parienté (2015) study whether access to microcredit changes the economic lives of rural households in Morocco. In their randomized evaluation, villages were assigned to receive access to Al Amana microfinance services earlier or later. Take-up was limited, so the paper distinguishes the effect of offering access from the effect on households that borrowed.

This project reproduces the non-financial outcomes in Table 9 of the authors' June 2019 specification. I reconstruct five outcomes from the supplied household questionnaires and estimate both the treated-household OLS and the instrumental-variables (IV) specifications. The four business-finance outcomes in Table 9 are not estimated because reproducing them requires the full price-imputation and activity-accounting pipeline in the authors' construction file. I also retain the direct credit-access estimate as a first-stage check.

## Data and empirical strategy

The [official article](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/app.20130535) studies 81 matched pairs of rural villages. One village within each pair was assigned early access to Al Amana. The comparison is randomized at the village level. The authors' endline input data include the treatment assignment, pair identifier, village identifier, outcomes, and sampling information. The supplied archive also contains the authors' June 2019 Stata analysis and outcome-construction files.

The analysis sample is the authors' high-propensity-to-borrow sample. I reconstruct it from the June 2019 analysis script: baseline random-sample households are excluded, with score-based reclassification for new endline households.

I estimate an OLS regression with village treatment and matched-pair fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by village. The main estimate is therefore an ITT: it measures the effect of access assignment, not the effect of borrowing on borrowers.

$$Y_{ivp}=\alpha+\beta T_{vp}+\lambda_p+\varepsilon_{ivp},$$

where $Y_{ivp}$ is the household credit outcome, $T_{vp}$ indicates that village $v$ in matched pair $p$ was assigned early access, and $\lambda_p$ are matched-pair fixed effects. The published specification adds household and respondent controls. I omit those controls here because reproducing their construction requires additional baseline transformations; the R model keeps the pair fixed effects and village-level clustering.

### Constructing the analysis sample

```{r load-data}
library(haven)

library_path <- file.path("data", "Data_Microcredit_Response", "Input")
if (!dir.exists(library_path)) {
  library_path <- file.path("outputs", "data", "Data_Microcredit_Response", "Input")
}
endline_file <- file.path(library_path, "Microcredit_EL_mini_anonym.dta")
baseline_file <- file.path(library_path, "Microcredit_BL_mini_anonym.dta")

endline <- read_dta(endline_file)
baseline <- read_dta(baseline_file)

# Keep only the variables needed for this outcome and the sample definition.
endline_small <- endline[, c("ident", "treatment", "paire", "demi_paire",
                             "wave", "newhh", "random5_end", "score2",
                             "score3", "client")]
baseline_small <- baseline[, c("ident", "random5")]

# Add the baseline random-sample flag to the endline observations.
analysis_data <- merge(endline_small, baseline_small,
                       by = "ident", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)

# Endline-only households were not in the baseline random sample.
analysis_data$random5[is.na(analysis_data$random5)] <- 0

# Retain the random-sample flag for designated endline additions.
endline_random <- !is.na(analysis_data$random5_end) &
  analysis_data$random5_end == 1 & analysis_data$newhh == 0
analysis_data$random5[endline_random] <- 1
analysis_data$random5_final <- analysis_data$random5

# Reclassify random-sample households above the new-household score threshold,
# separately for the score and survey waves used by the authors.
village_ids <- unique(analysis_data$demi_paire)
for (village_id in village_ids) {
  in_village <- which(analysis_data$demi_paire == village_id)
  new_households <- in_village[analysis_data$newhh[in_village] == 1]

  if (length(new_households) > 0) {
    min_score2 <- min(analysis_data$score2[new_households], na.rm = TRUE)
    min_score3 <- min(analysis_data$score3[new_households], na.rm = TRUE)

    reclass_wave2 <- in_village[analysis_data$random5[in_village] == 1 &
      analysis_data$wave[in_village] == 2 &
      !is.na(analysis_data$score2[in_village]) &
      analysis_data$score2[in_village] > min_score2]
    reclass_wave34 <- in_village[analysis_data$random5[in_village] == 1 &
      analysis_data$wave[in_village] == 34 &
      !is.na(analysis_data$score3[in_village]) &
      analysis_data$score3[in_village] > min_score3]

    analysis_data$random5_final[c(reclass_wave2, reclass_wave34)] <- 0
  }
}

analysis_data$sample_model <- analysis_data$random5_final == 0
sample_model <- subset(analysis_data, sample_model & !is.na(client))

sample_summary <- data.frame(
  "Endline observations" = nrow(endline),
  "High-propensity sample before outcome trimming" = nrow(sample_model),
  "Village clusters" = length(unique(sample_model$demi_paire)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(sample_summary, caption = "Reconstructed analysis sample")
```

The authors additionally trim 0.5 percent of observations using a rule based on extreme values across several financial outcomes. I have not reproduced that multivariate trimming rule because it depends on the full set of constructed outcomes. As a result, this sample contains 4,961 households, compared with 4,934 in the published table. I also omit the paper's baseline household and respondent controls. These differences mean this is a close partial replication rather than an exact reproduction of the full published specification.

## Empirical result: access to Al Amana credit

The first-stage check is that early access increased the probability of having an Al Amana loan among households in the high-propensity-to-borrow sample. The published comparison below is Table 2, Panel A, column 1.

```{r estimate-credit}
library(sandwich)

credit_model <- lm(client ~ treatment + factor(paire), data = sample_model)
cluster_vcov <- vcovCL(credit_model,
                       cluster = sample_model$demi_paire,
                       type = "HC1")

credit_result <- data.frame(
  Estimate = unname(coef(credit_model)["treatment"]),
  `Clustered standard error` = sqrt(cluster_vcov["treatment", "treatment"]),
  Observations = nobs(credit_model),
  `Control-group mean` = mean(sample_model$client[sample_model$treatment == 0]),
  check.names = FALSE
)

published_result <- data.frame(
  Estimate = 0.167,
  `Clustered standard error` = 0.012,
  Observations = 4934,
  `Control-group mean` = 0.000,
  check.names = FALSE
)

result_table <- data.frame(
  Outcome = "Al Amana loan (administrative measure)",
  `Published Table 2` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", published_result$Estimate,
                                published_result$`Clustered standard error`),
  ` Replication Estimation` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", credit_result$Estimate,
                         credit_result$`Clustered standard error`),
  `Published N` = published_result$Observations,
  `Replication N` = credit_result$Observations,
  `Published control mean` = sprintf("%.3f", published_result$`Control-group mean`),
  `Replication control mean` = sprintf("%.3f", credit_result$`Control-group mean`),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(result_table, caption = "Published and replicated credit-access estimate")
```

The replicated coefficient is 0.167 and the village-clustered standard error is 0.012 when rounded to three decimals, matching the published entry. The control-group mean is zero in both columns. The R sample is 27 observations larger because the authors' global financial-outlier trimming rule has not been reconstructed. The regression also omits baseline covariates, so matching to three decimals should be read as a useful replication check, not proof that every analysis choice is identical.

## Table 9: reconstructed non-financial outcomes

Table 9 reports an OLS estimate among borrowers in treatment villages (Panel A) and an IV estimate for the effect of borrowing among high-propensity households (Panel B). I reconstruct self-employment, day-labor and salaried income, weekly self-employment hours, weekly outside-work hours, and monthly consumption using the variable definitions in the June 2019 endline construction do-file. Each model includes matched-pair fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the village level. Panel A regresses each outcome on `client` among treated households. Panel B instruments `client` with randomized `treatment` in the full analysis sample.

The published models also include baseline household and respondent controls and apply a 0.5 percent multivariate financial-outlier trim. Those controls were created in intermediate files absent from the archive, and the outlier rule depends on the four financial outcomes not reconstructed here. Estimates below are therefore transparent partial reproductions, not exact replications. The table includes the published Table 9 entries for comparison.

```{r table9-outcomes}
library(ivreg)

raw <- endline
analysis_data$index <- match(analysis_data$ident, raw$ident)
raw <- raw[analysis_data$index, ]
raw$sample_model <- analysis_data$sample_model
raw$sample_model[is.na(raw$sample_model)] <- FALSE

row_sum_nonnegative <- function(dat, vars) {
  x <- as.data.frame(dat[, vars, drop = FALSE])
  x[] <- lapply(x, function(z) { z[z < 0] <- NA_real_; as.numeric(z) })
  n <- rowSums(!is.na(x))
  ans <- rowSums(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  # Stata's initialized row sums treat entirely blank item bundles as zero.
  ans[n == 0] <- 0
  ans
}

# Self-employment indicator: activity-specific production and livestock modules,
# following selfempl_agri/live/business in the source construction file.
count_yes <- function(dat, vars, predicate) {
  x <- as.data.frame(dat[, vars, drop = FALSE])
  rowSums(as.data.frame(lapply(x, predicate)), na.rm = TRUE)
}
agri_count <- count_yes(raw, paste0("e15_", 1:20), function(x) x == 1) +
  count_yes(raw, paste0("e25_", 1:13), function(x) x > 0) +
  count_yes(raw, paste0("e36_", 1:8), function(x) x == 1)
live_count <- count_yes(raw, paste0("f8_0_", 1:8), function(x) x == 1) +
  count_yes(raw, paste0("f15_0_", c(1:3, 5, 6, 4)), function(x) x == 1)
business_count <- count_yes(raw, paste0("d1_nom", 1:6), function(x) !is.na(x) & x != "" & x != "." )
business_count <- business_count + count_yes(raw, paste0("d2_", 1:6), function(x) x %in% 3:6)
raw$self_empl <- as.numeric(agri_count > 0 | live_count > 0 | business_count > 0)

# Annual income from day labor and salaried work.
raw$income_dep <- row_sum_nonnegative(raw, c(paste0("h11_", 1:22), paste0("h11c", 1:22)))

# Monthly total consumption from food, other non-durables, and durables.
food_vars <- c(paste0("h1_", c(1:14, 17, 18)), paste0("h2_", c(1:14, 17, 18)))
food <- row_sum_nonnegative(raw, food_vars) * 4.345
durables <- row_sum_nonnegative(raw, paste0("c4_", 1:31)) / 12
nondurables <- food + row_sum_nonnegative(raw, paste0("h1_", c(15, 16, 19:21))) * 4.345 +
  row_sum_nonnegative(raw, paste0("h2_", c(15, 19:21))) * 4.345 +
  row_sum_nonnegative(raw, paste0("h3_", c(1:9, 11:17))) +
  row_sum_nonnegative(raw, paste0("h4_", 1:10)) / 12 +
  row_sum_nonnegative(raw, paste0("h6_", 1:9)) / 12
nondurables[is.na(food) | food == 0] <- NA_real_
durables[is.na(food) | food == 0] <- NA_real_
raw$consumption <- nondurables + durables

# Weekly hours by activity, summed across members aged 16–65. For waves 2/3/4,
# activity hours are days times hours, classified by work relationship.
raw$hours_self_age16_65 <- NA_real_
raw$hours_outside_age16_65 <- NA_real_
for (r in seq_len(nrow(raw))) {
  self_person <- outside_person <- total_person <- rep(NA_real_, 24)
  wave <- raw$wave[r]
  js <- if (wave == 1) 1:11 else 1:24
  for (j in js) {
    age <- raw[[paste0("a7_", j)]][r]
    if (is.na(age) || age < 6 || age > 65) next
    sh <- oh <- chores <- 0
    if (wave == 1) {
      for (v in c(paste0("a12_p", j), paste0("a12_m", j))) {
        z <- raw[[v]][r]; if (!is.na(z) && z > 0 && z < 126) sh <- sh + z
      }
      z <- raw[[paste0("a14_", j)]][r]; if (!is.na(z) && z > 0 && z < 126) oh <- oh + z
      z <- raw[[paste0("a13_", j)]][r]; if (!is.na(z) && z > 0 && z < 126) chores <- chores + z
    } else if (wave %in% c(2, 34)) {
      for (i in 1:3) {
        rel <- raw[[paste0("h03_r", i, "_", j)]][r]
        hrs <- raw[[paste0("h05_a", i, "_", j)]][r]
        days <- raw[[paste0("h04_a", i, "_", j)]][r]
        h <- if (!is.na(hrs) && hrs >= 0 && hrs < 18 && !is.na(days) && days >= 0 && days <= 7) hrs * days else 0
        if (!is.na(rel) && rel %in% c(5, 7)) sh <- sh + h
        if (!is.na(rel) && (rel %in% 1:4 || rel %in% 6:9)) oh <- oh + h
      }
      days <- raw[[paste0("h07_", j)]][r]; hrs <- raw[[paste0("h08_", j)]][r]
      if (!is.na(days) && days >= 0 && days <= 7 && !is.na(hrs) && hrs >= 0 && hrs < 18) chores <- days * hrs
    }
    total_person[j] <- sh + oh + chores
    if (age >= 16) { self_person[j] <- sh; outside_person[j] <- oh }
  }
  too_many <- !is.na(total_person) & total_person > 126
  self_person[too_many] <- NA_real_; outside_person[too_many] <- NA_real_
  if (wave == 1) {
    nm <- sum(vapply(1:11, function(j) any(vapply(c(paste0("a12_m", j), paste0("a12_p", j), paste0("a13_", j), paste0("a14_", j)), function(v) !is.na(raw[[v]][r]), logical(1))), logical(1)))
    if (nm == 0) next
  } else if (wave %in% c(2, 34)) {
    nm <- sum(vapply(1:24, function(j) any(vapply(c(paste0("h01_", j), paste0("h03_a1_", j)), function(v) !is.na(raw[[v]][r]), logical(1))) || raw[[paste0("h02_", j)]][r] %in% c(1, 2), logical(1)))
    if (nm == 0) next
  } else next
  group <- which(vapply(1:24, function(j) { a <- raw[[paste0("a7_", j)]][r]; !is.na(a) && a >= 16 && a <= 65 }, logical(1)))
  # Stata's egen rsum returns zero when every eligible member's activity
  # component is missing; the outcome is missing only when the section itself
  # was not completed (the wave-specific checks above).
  raw$hours_self_age16_65[r] <- sum(self_person[group], na.rm = TRUE)
  raw$hours_outside_age16_65[r] <- sum(outside_person[group], na.rm = TRUE)
}

raw$client <- as.numeric(raw$client)
raw$treatment <- as.numeric(raw$treatment)
raw$paire <- as.factor(raw$paire)
raw$demi_paire <- as.factor(raw$demi_paire)
table9_vars <- c("self_empl", "income_dep", "hours_self_age16_65", "hours_outside_age16_65", "consumption")
published <- data.frame(
  Outcome = table9_vars,
  `Table 9 Panel A` = c("0.019 (0.016)", "-1,263 (1,138)", "6.6 (3.0)", "-3.1 (3.1)", "482 (192)"),
  `Table 9 Panel B` = c("-0.091 (0.060)", "-6,281 (2,866)", "3.6 (8.0)", "-18.2 (5.8)", "-274 (278)"),
  `Published N A` = c(2448, 2448, 2440, 2440, 2444),
  `Published N B` = c(4934, 4934, 4918, 4918, 4924), check.names = FALSE
)
results <- lapply(seq_along(table9_vars), function(k) {
  y <- table9_vars[k]
  dA <- raw[raw$sample_model & raw$treatment == 1 & !is.na(raw[[y]]) & !is.na(raw$client), ]
  dB <- raw[raw$sample_model & !is.na(raw[[y]]) & !is.na(raw$client) & !is.na(raw$treatment), ]
  fA <- as.formula(paste(y, "~ client + factor(paire)"))
  mA <- lm(fA, data = dA)
  vA <- sandwich::vcovCL(mA, cluster = dA$demi_paire, type = "HC1")
  fB <- as.formula(paste(y, "~ client + factor(paire) | treatment + factor(paire)"))
  mB <- ivreg::ivreg(fB, data = dB)
  vB <- sandwich::vcovCL(mB, cluster = dB$demi_paire, type = "HC1")
  data.frame(Outcome = y,
    `Published Table 9 A` = published$`Table 9 Panel A`[k],
    `Replication A` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", coef(mA)["client"], sqrt(vA["client", "client"])),
    `N A` = nobs(mA), `Published Table 9 B` = published$`Table 9 Panel B`[k],
    `Replication B` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", coef(mB)["client"], sqrt(vB["client", "client"])),
    `N B` = nobs(mB), check.names = FALSE)
})
table9_results <- do.call(rbind, results)
knitr::kable(table9_results, caption = "Table 9: published and reconstructed non-financial estimates")
```

The reconstructed estimates use no baseline controls, unlike the published models. The published sample sizes also differ because the archive does not include the authors' processed outcome file or the multivariate trimming result. Interpret differences as evidence of incomplete specification matching, not as a correction to the published estimates.

## Limitations

This project reproduces five of Table 9's nine outcome definitions and estimates both reported panels. The four financial activity outcomes (assets, output/sales, expenses, and profit) are omitted because their construction requires price imputation and multi-module aggregation. The archived inputs do not include the authors' processed endline outcome file. Baseline household and respondent controls, and the 0.5 percent multivariate trimming rule, are omitted. Exact replication is therefore not claimed.

## Conclusion

The project now extends beyond the first-stage credit-access check to five non-financial Table 9 outcomes. The table provides estimates for both panels alongside the published benchmarks. Differences from the published estimates may arise from the omission of baseline controls and the original trimming procedure, as well as potential discrepancies in outcome construction and sample composition. Without fully reproducing the original specification, the contribution of each factor cannot be determined. The four financial outcomes are omitted rather than approximated.

## References

Crépon, Bruno, Florencia Devoto, Esther Duflo, and William Parienté. 2015. “Estimating the Impact of Microcredit on Those Who Take It Up: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment in Morocco.” *American Economic Journal: Applied Economics* 7 (1): 123–150. [Article page and supplemental materials](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/app.20130535). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20130535).

Crépon, Bruno, Florencia Devoto, Esther Duflo, and William Parienté. 2019. *Data and Code for: Estimating the Impact of Microcredit on Those Who Take It Up: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment in Morocco*. Data and code archive supplied with this project, containing the anonymized baseline and endline Stata files and the authors' June 2019 construction and analysis files.

The published comparison is from Table 2, Panel A, column 1 of Crépon et al. (2015). Data variable labels and sample-selection steps were checked against the supplied authors' data and analysis files.
